cards.q: What makes a computer different from a calculator?
cards.a:
It follows a stored program that can be changed

A calculator is built for one job. A computer runs whatever list of instructions it is given, so one machine can do many different jobs.

cards.q: Which part of a computer carries out the instructions?
cards.a:
The CPU

The CPU (central processing unit) does the processing. Memory holds the program and data it works on.

cards.q: What is a bit?
cards.a:
A single 0 or 1

"Bit" is short for binary digit: one switch that is off or on. Everything inside a computer is stored as patterns of bits.

cards.q: What did the Jacquard loom contribute to computing?
cards.a:
Instructions on swappable punched cards

The instructions were stored outside the machine: changing the cards changed the pattern without changing the loom, separating hardware and software.

cards.q: Which part of the Analytical Engine is the same idea as a modern CPU?
cards.a:
The mill

The mill did the arithmetic. The store was the memory.

cards.q: What did Ada Lovelace write in 1843?
cards.a:
The first published computer program

Her Note G was a step-by-step method for the Analytical Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers.

cards.q: What did Turing's 1936 paper show?
cards.a:
That one universal machine can run any program

A simple "universal" machine can follow the rules of any other machine, because the program is just more data for it to read. That is the idea behind every general-purpose computer.

cards.q: What problem did the stored-program design solve?
cards.a:
Changing the program meant rewiring by hand

ENIAC had to be rewired for every new problem; storing the program in memory made changing it as easy as loading data. Nearly every computer since the Manchester Baby (1948) works this way.

cards.q: Which of these was built from relays?
cards.a:
The Z3

Zuse's Z3 used about 2,600 relays. Colossus and ENIAC used vacuum tubes.

cards.q: What did the integrated circuit make possible?
cards.a:
Many transistors made together on one chip

The transistors and their connections are made together on one piece of silicon: no more soldering thousands of separate parts by hand.
cards.lessonTitle: Transistors, Chips and the Personal Computer

cards.q: What was special about the Intel 4004?
cards.a:
It was a whole CPU on one chip

The first commercial microprocessor, from 1971, with about 2,300 transistors.
cards.lessonTitle: Transistors, Chips and the Personal Computer

cards.q: Roughly how often did Moore's law say transistor counts double?
cards.a:
About every two years

Moore's 1975 estimate. It held for decades, and has slowed only recently.
cards.lessonTitle: Transistors, Chips and the Personal Computer

cards.q: Why does a program built for an x86-64 PC not run directly on an ARM phone?
cards.a:
The two chips use different instruction sets

Each instruction set has its own machine code, so the program has to be built (translated) for each one.

cards.q: What is a CPU core?
cards.a:
One complete processor on the chip

A modern chip has several cores working side by side, so it can run several things at the same time.

cards.q: Why is a GPU good at drawing pictures and AI maths?
cards.a:
Thousands of simple cores work in parallel

Pixels and the maths of AI are both huge numbers of similar, independent sums, which many simple cores can do at once.

cards.q: Why do computers use two voltage levels instead of ten?
cards.a:
Two levels far apart are very hard to confuse, even with electrical noise

Reliability is the main reason. Noise easily confuses levels that are close together.

cards.q: How many different patterns can 4 bits make?
cards.a:
16

2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. Each extra bit doubles the count.

cards.q: What does the bit pattern 01000001 mean?
cards.a:
Whatever the program reads it as

Bits have no meaning by themselves. The program decides: it could be 65, the letter A, or something else.

cards.q: What is 0b1010 in decimal?
What is 13 in binary?
cards.a:
1101

8 + 4 + 1 = 13, so the 8, 4 and 1 places hold a 1: 1101.

cards.q: What is the largest number 8 bits can hold?
cards.a:
255

All eight bits on: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255. With 0, that is 256 different values.

cards.q: Which binary numbers are odd?
cards.a:
Those that end in 1

The rightmost place is worth 1; every other place is worth an even number.

cards.q: How many bits are in a byte?
cards.a:
8

8 bits make a byte; 4 make a nibble.

cards.q: A drive sold as 500 GB shows as about 465 GB in Windows. Why?
cards.a:
The box counts in 1,000s; Windows in 1,024s

500,000,000,000 bytes ÷ 1,073,741,824 ≈ 465.7 GiB, which Windows labels "GB".

cards.q: Roughly how many MB per second does a 400 Mbps connection carry at most?
cards.a:
50

Mbps is megabits. Divide by 8 bits per byte: 400 ÷ 8 = 50 MB per second.

cards.q: How many bits are needed to give each of 300 students a different number?
cards.a:
9

2⁸ = 256 is too few; 2⁹ = 512 is enough.

cards.q: What is 0x1F in decimal?
How many bits does one hex digit stand for?
cards.a:
4

16 = 2⁴. That is why hex lines up so neatly with binary.

cards.q: What is 0b1100_0011 in hex?
How many hex digits does one byte need?
cards.a:
2

A byte is 8 bits, two groups of four: 00 to FF.

cards.q: What is 0b0110 + 0b0011?
In 8 bits, unsigned, what is 200 + 100?
cards.a:
44

300 needs 9 bits. 300 − 256 = 44 is what is left in 8 bits.

cards.q: Read 0b1111_1110 as a signed 8-bit number.
Why do computers use two's complement for negative numbers?
cards.a:
One adding circuit works for both signs

The same adder handles positive and negative numbers, so subtraction needs no extra circuit: "flip, add one, and add".

cards.q: What is the largest unsigned 16-bit number?
Why could a 32-bit computer use only about 4 GB of memory?
cards.a:
32-bit addresses can number only 2³² = about 4.3 billion bytes

Each byte needs its own address, and 32 bits give 2³² different ones.

cards.q: A little-endian computer stores the 16-bit number 0x1234. Which byte comes first in memory?
cards.a:
0x34

Little-endian puts the lowest (little) end first, and it stores whole bytes: 0x34 then 0x12. The digits inside a byte are never swapped, so 0x43 is wrong.

cards.q: What happens to a signed 32-bit seconds counter in January 2038?
cards.a:
It wraps to a large negative number

2,147,483,647 + 1 wraps to −2,147,483,648, like 127 + 1 in 8 bits, so the date reads as 1901.

cards.q: In ASCII, the letter C is 67. What is c?
cards.a:
99

Lower case is upper case plus 32: 67 + 32 = 99.

cards.q: The character '5' is stored as which number in ASCII?
cards.a:
53

The digits start at 48: '0' is 48, so '5' is 53. Its value is 53 − 48 = 5.

cards.q: Why did UTF-8 become the standard?
cards.a:
It covers all of Unicode and fits ASCII

It can store every Unicode character, and plain ASCII text is already valid UTF-8, so old text keeps working.

cards.q: How many bytes does UTF-8 use for the letter é (U+00E9)?
cards.a:
2

Code points from U+0080 to U+07FF take two bytes.

cards.q: What does print("Hi") actually hand to the operating system?
cards.a:
The bytes 72, 105 and 10

Just numbers: the UTF-8 bytes of the text, plus a new line.
cards.lessonTitle: How Text Gets on the Screen

cards.q: Where do the shapes of letters come from?
cards.a:
A font, which maps each character to a glyph

The terminal or app looks up each character's glyph in a font and draws it as pixels.
cards.lessonTitle: How Text Gets on the Screen

cards.q: What does the byte 10 do in terminal output?
cards.a:
Starts a new line

10 is line feed, written \n in most languages.
cards.lessonTitle: How Text Gets on the Screen

cards.q: What is 0b0.11 in decimal?
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not exactly 0.3 in most languages?
cards.a:
0.1 and 0.2 cannot be stored exactly in binary

One tenth repeats forever in binary, so only an approximation is stored, and the two small errors add up.

cards.q: What is the safe way to store an amount of money?
cards.a:
As a whole number of cents

Integers are exact, so £12.34 as 1234 pence never drifts. A decimal type works too.

cards.q: About how many significant decimal digits does a 64-bit double keep?
cards.a:
15 to 17

52 bits of fraction give about 15 to 17 decimal digits.

cards.q: What colour is #00FF00?
cards.a:
Bright green

Red 00, green FF (255), blue 00.

cards.q: How many bytes does an uncompressed 100 × 100 RGB image take?
cards.a:
30,000

100 × 100 pixels × 3 bytes.

cards.q: What is the difference between lossless and lossy compression?
cards.a:
Only lossless gives back the exact original

Lossy compression throws away detail people barely notice, to save more space. PNG is lossless; JPEG is lossy.

cards.q: Why is CD audio sampled 44,100 times a second?
cards.a:
It is over twice the highest pitch we hear

The sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency. People hear up to about 20,000 Hz, so the rate needs to be over 40,000.

cards.q: What is a file?
cards.a:
A name and a row of bytes

The bytes carry no label. The file's format, and the program reading it, decide what the bytes mean.

cards.q: A file starts with the bytes 25 50 44 46. What is it probably?
cards.a:
A PDF document

25 50 44 46 is "%PDF".

cards.q: You rename song.mp3 to song.txt. What happens to its bytes?
cards.a:
Nothing: only the name changed

The extension is just part of the name.

cards.q: In a hex dump, what does the offset column show?
cards.a:
How far into the file each row starts

Rows of 16 bytes, so the offsets go 0, 0x10, 0x20, ...

cards.q: What does A XOR B give when both inputs are 1?
cards.a:
0

XOR is 1 when exactly one input is 1, and both 1 is not "exactly one". The inputs can be swapped without changing the result.

cards.q: How many rows does the truth table of a 3-input gate have?
cards.a:
8

2³ = 8: every input pattern once.

cards.q: What is 12 & 10 in Python?
cards.a:
8

1100 & 1010 = 1000, which is 8. (12 | 10 would be 14, and 12 ^ 10 would be 6.)

cards.q: How do you make NOT A from a NAND gate?
cards.a:
Connect A to both inputs: A NAND A

A NAND A is NOT (A AND A), which is NOT A.

cards.q: Which gate gives the sum bit of a half adder?
cards.a:
XOR

1 + 1 = 10: sum 0, carry 1. Sum is XOR, carry is AND.

cards.q: What does a full adder have that a half adder does not?
cards.a:
A carry in from the column to its right

Every column but the first has a carry coming in.

cards.q: With a 4-bit adder, what is 9 + 8?
cards.a:
1

17 = 10001 needs 5 bits. The top carry is lost, leaving 0001 = 1.

cards.q: How does an adder do subtraction?
cards.a:
It adds the two's complement of b

It flips the bits of the second number and sets the first carry in to 1: a − b = a + (NOT b) + 1.

cards.q: What makes a latch able to remember a bit?
cards.a:
Its outputs feed back into its inputs

Feedback gives the circuit two stable states, so it holds whichever it was set to.

cards.q: How does a program find a particular byte in RAM?
cards.a:
By its address, a number

Memory is a numbered row of bytes. Any address can be read directly.

cards.q: What happens to the contents of RAM when the computer is switched off?
cards.a:
They are lost

RAM is volatile. Saving copies data to storage, which is not.

cards.q: A 4-byte integer is stored starting at address 0x2000. Which addresses does it use?
cards.a:
0x2000, 0x2001, 0x2002 and 0x2003

One byte per address, four neighbouring addresses.

cards.q: What does the program counter hold?
cards.a:
The address of the next instruction to fetch

It is the CPU's bookmark in the program.

cards.q: In the tiny computer, what does the number 412 mean?
cards.a:
STORE 12: copy A into cell 12

The hundreds digit (4) is the operation; 12 is the address.

cards.q: How is a loop made in machine code?
cards.a:
With jumps: back to repeat, and out to stop

JUMP goes back to an earlier instruction; a conditional jump such as JUMPZ leaves when the counter reaches zero.

cards.q: Why can the tiny computer's program be changed by changing numbers in memory?
cards.a:
The program is numbers in the same memory

The program is stored in the same memory as the data: the stored-program design of 1.03.

cards.q: What is machine code?
cards.a:
A program as the bytes the CPU actually reads and executes

Every program ends up as machine code before the CPU can run it.

cards.q: In B8 2A 00 00 00 (mov eax, 42), why is 42 written as 2A 00 00 00?
cards.a:
It is 0x2A in 4 bytes, lowest first

0x2A = 42, stored as a 32-bit number, and x86 stores numbers little-endian: lowest byte first.

cards.q: Why does an x86-64 program not run directly on an ARM64 CPU?
cards.a:
The two encode instructions differently

Each instruction set has its own machine code, so the same bytes mean different things.

cards.q: What does an assembler do?
cards.a:
Turns instruction names into machine code

It translates instructions written as short names into bytes: `mov eax, 42` in, B8 2A 00 00 00 out.

cards.q: Why do CPUs have caches?
cards.a:
RAM is far slower than the CPU

Recently used data is kept in a small fast memory close to the CPU. A cache hit costs about a nanosecond; a trip to RAM about a hundred.

cards.q: What is a cache line?
cards.a:
The block fetched at a time, often 64 bytes

Fetching the neighbours along with the requested byte pays off because of spatial locality.

cards.q: Which is usually faster for a big grid of numbers stored row after row?
cards.a:
Reading it row by row

Row by row reads memory in order and uses every byte of each cache line.

cards.q: What is the relationship between assembly and machine code?
cards.a:
Each line is one instruction, written as a name

Nearly every assembly line is one machine instruction written as a name instead of numbers, so an assembler translates it almost one to one.

cards.q: What does a label like loop: give the programmer?
cards.a:
A name for an address

The assembler works out the address and keeps it up to date: no more recalculating jump addresses by hand.

cards.q: Why is there no single assembly language?
cards.a:
Each CPU family has its own instructions

x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V each have their own instructions, so each has its own assembly.

cards.q: What did FORTRAN let scientists do?
cards.a:
Write formulas that compile to fast code

FORmula TRANslation: formulas like Y = (A + B) * C / 2.0, turned into machine code by a compiler whose speed is why it caught on.

cards.q: Who argued that computers could understand English-like words, and led work on early compilers?
cards.a:
Grace Hopper

A-0 in 1952 and FLOW-MATIC, which shaped COBOL.

cards.q: Which idea came from Lisp?
cards.a:
Garbage collection

Memory is freed automatically when no longer used. Python, Java, JavaScript and C# all collect garbage.

cards.q: What is a compiler?
cards.a:
A program that translates code to machine code

It translates a high-level language into machine code; one line can become many machine instructions.

cards.q: What does a compiler produce?
cards.a:
Machine code, before the program runs

C, C++, Rust and Go compile ahead of time into an executable.

cards.q: What is a virtual machine in the sense of the JVM?
cards.a:
A program that runs bytecode

Bytecode is an instruction set for an imaginary computer; the JVM runs Java bytecode on whatever real computer it is on.

cards.q: Why can JavaScript be fast despite starting as source code?
cards.a:
Its engine compiles hot code while it runs

The engine JIT-compiles the parts that run often into machine code on the fly.

cards.q: When is an error in an interpreted language's code often found?
cards.a:
Only when that line actually runs

There is no separate compile step to check everything first.

cards.q: What was new about rewriting Unix in C in 1973?
cards.a:
The system could move to new computers

Portability: an operating system in a high-level language could be moved by writing a C compiler for the new machine. Before, operating systems were written in assembly for one machine.

cards.q: Why is C called a "portable assembly"?
cards.a:
It is close to the machine yet portable

Pointers and predictable code keep it low-level, yet it compiles for many CPU families.

cards.q: Which operating system is a descendant of BSD Unix?
cards.a:
macOS

macOS and iOS come from NeXTSTEP, which was built on BSD. Linux is Unix-like but written from scratch.

cards.q: Which language added classes to C?
cards.a:
C++

Bjarne Stroustrup's "C with Classes" became C++ in 1985.
cards.lessonTitle: The Family Tree of Modern Languages

cards.q: What is the main idea of Rust?
cards.a:
C's speed with memory bugs caught early

Rust aims for the speed of C and C++, and its compiler checks who owns each piece of memory, catching memory mistakes before the program runs.
cards.lessonTitle: The Family Tree of Modern Languages

cards.q: What does "statically typed" mean?
cards.a:
Types are checked before the program runs

C, Java, Rust and TypeScript check types at compile time; Python and JavaScript at run time.
cards.lessonTitle: The Family Tree of Modern Languages

cards.q: What is the CPython interpreter itself written in?
cards.a:
C

CPython is a C program, compiled to machine code.
cards.lessonTitle: One Line of Code All the Way Down

cards.q: Why does a program use a system call to print?
cards.a:
Only the system may touch devices

User-mode programs cannot use hardware like the screen directly, so they must ask the operating system.
cards.lessonTitle: One Line of Code All the Way Down

cards.q: Which bytes does print("Hi") hand to the operating system?
cards.a:
72, 105 and 10

UTF-8 for H and i, plus the new line.
cards.lessonTitle: One Line of Code All the Way Down

cards.q: What is the kernel?
cards.a:
The core of the OS, which runs the hardware

It is the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly. Everything else runs in user mode and asks it through system calls.

cards.q: Why can an ordinary app not read the disk directly?
cards.a:
In user mode the CPU forbids it

The app must ask the kernel with a system call, and the kernel checks every request, which keeps programs safe from each other.

cards.q: Why does one app crashing usually not crash the whole computer?
cards.a:
Each app is kept in its own memory

The kernel stops the crashed app and cleans up; user-mode isolation contains the damage.

cards.q: What is the difference between a program and a process?
cards.a:
A program is a file; a process is it running

A process has its own memory and state, and one program can be running as several processes at once.

cards.q: What does a context switch do?
cards.a:
Swaps one thread's registers for another's

It saves one thread's registers and loads another's, so the second carries on where it stopped. That is how the scheduler shares a core.

cards.q: Why might two threads adding 1 to the same counter lose updates?
cards.a:
Both can read the old value first

If both read before either writes back, one increment is lost: a race condition. Locks prevent it.

cards.q: Why is CPU usage often low even with hundreds of threads?
cards.a:
Most threads are waiting

Only ready threads use the CPU, and waiting for input, files or the network takes no CPU time.

cards.q: What does virtual memory give each process?
cards.a:
Its own private range of addresses

The CPU translates each process's addresses to real RAM, so two processes can use the same virtual address and land in different places.

cards.q: With 4 KiB pages, what is the offset part of virtual address 0x5123?
cards.a:
0x123

The lowest 12 bits (three hex digits) are the offset within the page.

cards.q: Why does following a null pointer crash the program?
cards.a:
Address 0 is deliberately left unmapped

The CPU faults and the kernel stops the program. The crash is deliberate: it catches the bug immediately.

cards.q: What happens when RAM runs out but a program needs more?
cards.a:
Unused pages are moved out to disk

Swapping frees RAM and brings pages back when needed. It is slow, which is why a computer with too little RAM feels sluggish.

cards.q: What does a disk itself know about files?
cards.a:
Nothing: it stores numbered blocks

The file system, kernel software, tracks which blocks belong to which file and organises them into files and folders.

cards.q: What is file descriptor 1?
cards.a:
Standard output

0 is standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error.

cards.q: What does a driver do?
cards.a:
Lets the kernel control one kind of device

Every device model speaks differently; its driver translates through a standard interface.

cards.q: Where does the very first code run after power-on come from?
cards.a:
Firmware in a chip on the motherboard

RAM is empty at power-on; the CPU starts at an address wired to the firmware chip (UEFI or BIOS).
cards.lessonTitle: Booting: From Power Button to Desktop

cards.q: What is the boot loader's job?
cards.a:
To load the kernel and start it

It finds the kernel on the disk, loads it into RAM and jumps to it. Examples: GRUB, Windows Boot Manager, iBoot.
cards.lessonTitle: Booting: From Power Button to Desktop

cards.q: On Linux, what is process number 1?
cards.a:
The first user-mode process

Usually systemd, which starts everything else; every other process descends from it.
cards.lessonTitle: Booting: From Power Button to Desktop

cards.q: What is the difference between sleep and hibernate?
cards.a:
Sleep keeps RAM powered; hibernate does not

Hibernate saves RAM to disk and powers off completely. Sleep wakes instantly but uses a little power.
cards.lessonTitle: Booting: From Power Button to Desktop

cards.q: Why is data sent as packets?
cards.a:
Each can route and be resent on its own

Small packets travel separately, take different routes around failures, and are resent individually if lost, which makes the internet robust.

cards.q: What does DNS do?
cards.a:
Turns names into IP addresses

DNS turns names like example.com into addresses: the internet's phone book.

cards.q: How many bits is an IPv4 address?
cards.a:
32

Four bytes, which is why there are only about 4.3 billion. IPv6 uses 128 bits.

cards.q: What does TCP add on top of IP?
cards.a:
Reliable, in-order delivery

TCP resends lost packets and puts them back in order. UDP skips those guarantees to be quicker.
